paper.citation: Oldham JR, Lanois CJ, Caccese JB, et al. Association Between Collision Sport Career Duration and Gait Performance in Male Collegiate Student-Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2022;[volume and issue not stated in extracted text]:1-8.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional study of 168 male NCAA Division I student-athletes from football, lacrosse, ice hockey and wrestling (mean age 19.2 +/- 1.3 years; career duration 10.6 +/- 3.0 years). Single- and dual-task gait speed and stride length were measured with inertial measurement units at preseason baseline testing, and career duration was analysed with linear regression adjusted for concussion history and height.
paper.tldr: In 168 male collegiate collision-sport athletes, longer career duration was not associated with single- or dual-task gait, but the cross-sectional design cannot show effects that may appear later in life.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study at two NCAA Division I institutions, with gait assessed during preseason baseline concussion testing. Participants completed five single-task and five dual-task 10-m walks, with the dual task being serial working-memory questions, and gait was recorded with three inertial measurement units. Career duration was calculated as age minus estimated age of first exposure, or self-reported career duration at one site, and entered as a continuous variable in linear regression.
paper.findings: Career duration was not significantly associated with single-task gait speed (b = -0.004; P = .35) or dual-task gait speed (b = -0.003; P = .57), nor with stride length, cognitive accuracy or dual-task cost. Mean single-task gait speed was 1.16 +/- 0.16 m/s and dual-task gait speed 1.02 +/- 0.17 m/s, with eta-squared effect sizes of 0.017 or less for all gait outcomes.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so it cannot show how gait changes over a career or across the lifespan. Career duration was largely self-reported, continuous participation was not verified, differences in collision rules across sports were not captured, and the sample was male, collegiate-aged and restricted to participants with careers of at least 5 years.
paper.practicalImplications: Gait speed and stride length can be used as reference measures of dynamic postural control in collegiate collision-sport athletes, and they did not vary with career length in this sample. The finding should not be read as evidence that cumulative head-impact exposure is harmless over time, so standard baseline and post-injury assessment should continue.
paper.athleteDev: The study provides reference values for single-task (1.16 m/s) and dual-task (1.02 m/s) gait speed in collegiate male collision-sport athletes, which staff can use as context when interpreting IMU gait testing. It does not evaluate training or performance interventions.
paper.rtp: It cannot be used for return-to-sport decisions: it assessed baseline gait in athletes without a current concussion and did not examine post-injury gait, symptom recovery or return timelines. The reference values should not be used as post-concussion benchmarks.
